title: The deadliest animal on Earth
text: If you were asked to name the most dangerous animal in the world, you would probably think of a shark, a lion or perhaps a crocodile. These predators certainly have sharp teeth and a frightening reputation, but together they kill only a few hundred people a year. The real champion is far smaller, weighs less than a grain of rice and may well be flying around your bedroom tonight: the mosquito.

Mosquitoes are not dangerous because of their bite, which is usually nothing more than an itchy red spot. The problem is what they can carry. When a mosquito feeds on the blood of an infected person or animal, tiny parasites or viruses can travel into its body. The next time it bites someone, it may pass them on. In this way, mosquitoes spread diseases such as malaria, dengue and yellow fever, which together cause hundreds of thousands of deaths every year, mainly in tropical countries.

Surprisingly, only female mosquitoes bite. Males live on the sugar found in flowers and fruit, and so do females most of the time. However, a female needs the protein in blood in order to produce her eggs. To find a victim, she relies on an impressive set of senses. She can detect the carbon dioxide we breathe out from several metres away, and as she gets closer, she follows the heat and the smell of our skin. That is why some people seem to be bitten far more often than others.

Their bite is also more sophisticated than it looks. A mosquito does not simply stab the skin with a single needle. Its mouth contains six thin parts that work together: some cut through the skin, one searches for a blood vessel and another injects saliva. The saliva stops the blood from clotting and, conveniently for the insect, it also makes the bite almost painless at first. By the time we notice the itch, the mosquito has usually flown away.

Fighting such a tiny enemy has never been easy. For decades, people have relied on insecticides, mosquito nets and draining the still water where mosquitoes lay their eggs. Nets treated with insecticide have saved millions of lives, especially among young children. However, many mosquitoes have become resistant to the chemicals, so scientists are looking for new solutions.

Some of these solutions sound like science fiction. In several countries, researchers have released mosquitoes carrying a natural type of bacteria called Wolbachia, which makes it much harder for the insects to pass on certain viruses. Others are developing genetically modified mosquitoes that produce offspring unable to survive. In addition, the first vaccines against malaria have recently been approved, which many experts see as a historic step.

Not everyone agrees that we should try to get rid of mosquitoes completely, however. They are food for birds, bats, fish and frogs, and some ecologists warn that removing them could have consequences we cannot predict. For now, the battle continues, and it is a reminder that in nature, size is not everything. The most dangerous creature on the planet is not the one with the biggest teeth, but the one we can barely see.
